title: Concurrency-safe class design
idea: Designing for concurrency means making every check-then-act on shared state happen as one unit, so overlapping requests cannot both pass the check.

analogy.text: Two shop assistants both see one mug left on the stock list, go to the back room, and both promise it to a customer.
analogy.breaks: In Node the trip to the back room is an `await`, not a thread.

points: Node runs JavaScript on one thread, but `await` lets other requests run between lines.
A check made before an `await` can be stale when you act.
Let the store enforce the rule with a unique key or a version check.
Prefer immutable values and fewer shared fields: less shared state means fewer races.

steps.caption: Order A starts. One mug is left in the shared stock store.
A reaches `await db()` and parks. The thread is now free for other work.
Order B runs in that gap and parks at the same `await`.
A's read finishes first; B is still waiting on its read.
A's check passes: one mug left. A starts its write and parks again.
B's check also passes: A has not written yet. Both hold a stale count.
A's write lands. A is told the mug is sold.
B's write lands too. Both were told 'sold': the stock is now -1.
The fix: the store rejects B's write because the version changed. B rereads and sees sold out.

code.title: Store-enforced rule
code.caption: You met this race and the `KeyedLock` in the booking case studies (c03-t05, c03-t08). Here the store refuses a stale write instead.

walk.text: Each row carries a `version` that changes on every write.
`update` writes only if the version is still the one the caller read.
A refused write means someone else won: read again and recheck.
Cap the retries so a busy item cannot loop forever.

code.title: Short, synchronous section
code.caption: Do slow work first. Then check and write with no `await` between them.

walk.text: No `await` inside `reserve`, so no other request can run between check and write.
Callers get a frozen value, not a handle on shared state.
The slow price lookup happens before the short section, not inside it.

pitfalls: Never check, then `await`, then act on the check without a lock or a constraint.
Do not retry a refused version check forever; cap retries and report the conflict.
Keep locked sections short and never `await` another lock inside one, or you risk deadlock.

quiz.why: All three calls read `n` as 0 before any of them resumes after `await`. Each then writes 0 + 1: a lost update.

takeaway: Make check-then-act one unit: a lock, a transaction, or a constraint.

starters: If Node is single-threaded, how can it have race conditions?
How would I stop overselling when the service runs on several servers?
When should I use optimistic locking with a version field instead of a lock?
